title: Greg Pikitis

jokes.text: Leslie confronting Greg Pikitis with dramatic gravitas: 'I'm here to tell you that this year it ends.'
jokes.setup: Leslie approaches a teenage boy in what seems like a mundane parks department context
jokes.punchline: She delivers a hyper-dramatic 'this year it ends' threat as if confronting a mob boss, not a teenager who TPs a statue
jokes.explanation: Perfect Leslie character comedy — her outsized seriousness about a trivial matter is the entire joke. The line 'it ends today' is absurdly grandiose for a Parks lady talking to a teen. Strong character integration because only Leslie would deliver this with complete sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Greg
dialogue.line: The Parks lady? Really?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes. The Parks lady. That's me. I'm the Parks lady and I'm proud of it.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head: 'He's like an invisible, adolescent, James Bond super villain criminal mastermind.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is describing a teenager who vandalizes a park statue every Halloween
jokes.punchline: She escalates the description to 'James Bond super villain criminal mastermind' — a comically overwrought label for a teenager's seasonal prank
jokes.explanation: A great Leslie Knope joke — the escalating string of descriptors ('invisible, adolescent, James Bond super villain criminal mastermind') is funny through absurd accumulation. The word 'adolescent' wedged in there is the funniest beat, deflating the hyperbole mid-sentence. Highly quotable and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This kid was a legendary prankster. Started small with classic stuff - fake spiders, switching the sugar and salt shakers. But then it escalated. He hacked into the school's PA system and played recordings of his own voice making increasingly threatening announcements. 'Attention students, I am now in the ventilation system.' 'I can see you from the shadows.' By senior year, they had to call in a crisis negotiator. The kid had rappelled down from the gymnasium rafters during the spring assembly while simultaneously live-tweeting his own location to throw off pursuit. The FBI showed up. The actual FBI. And you know what the punchline was? He was just trying to ask Jennifer Martinez to prom.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head immediately undercuts herself: 'Or maybe someone else is doing it, but I really feel like it's this kid.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just delivered a grandiose description of Greg Pikitis as a criminal mastermind
jokes.punchline: She immediately admits she has no proof and it might just be her gut feeling
jokes.explanation: Sharp structural comedy — the immediate deflation after the 'super villain' build-up. The show smartly has Leslie acknowledge she might be wrong, which makes her obsession funnier and more human. Good economy: one sentence does all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But I really feel like he's a criminal mastermind.

jokes.text: Greg Pikitis, after Leslie's dramatic confrontation: 'Thanks for stopping by, Leslie. You look great.' Leslie: 'Thank you. Ends today.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just delivered her dramatic 'it ends today' ultimatum to a smirking teenager
jokes.punchline: Greg dismisses her with casual pleasantries; Leslie reflexively says 'thank you' before catching herself and repeating her threat — revealing she's already been flustered
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Greg's casual 'you look great' completely disarms Leslie's theatrical threat, and her automatic 'thank you' before recalibrating is perfect character comedy — showing she's already lost the psychological battle with this kid. The callback to 'ends today' works beautifully. Highly quotable, economical, and reveals both characters instantly.

dialogue.speaker: Greg
dialogue.line: That's a very nice blazer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Thank you. Now, as I was saying, I will destroy you.

jokes.text: Ann's talking head: 'Hey, slutty teenage girls dressed as sexy kittens, pump your own stomachs this year.'
jokes.setup: Ann is explaining why Halloween is her favorite holiday — 'I don't have to work'
jokes.punchline: She addresses 'slutty teenage girls dressed as sexy kittens' and tells them to 'pump your own stomachs this year' — a nurse's dark, professional version of a holiday greeting
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-specific joke — only a nurse would have this particular holiday grievance, and the specific image of 'sexy kittens pumping their own stomachs' is darkly funny and surprising. Strong originality. The casual delivery makes it land harder. One of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: Ann mentions the party is invite-only, Tom immediately appears asking 'What's going on, cupcake?' — he was clearly not invited.
jokes.setup: Ann specifies 'the people in this room now are the people I invited... don't tell anybody.' Someone immediately asks 'Who's not invited?'
jokes.punchline: Tom bursts in with 'What's going on, cupcake? Excited about the party tonight.' — clearly having been told by Jerry
jokes.explanation: A functional comedic beat — the timing of Tom's entrance right after Ann's edict is clean situational comedy. 'Cupcake' is good Tom character voice. Not especially original but well-executed structurally.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Who's not invited?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Me.

jokes.text: Tom, upon learning he wasn't originally invited: 'Jerry already told me. Can't wait to see how tiny your costume is.'
jokes.setup: Tom has crashed the party after Jerry told him despite Ann's instructions
jokes.punchline: Tom is completely unbothered about crashing and immediately pivots to complimenting/objectifying Ann — classic Tom deflection
jokes.explanation: Tom's complete shamelessness about crashing is character-consistent and mildly funny. The 'tiny costume' line is creepy-Tom in miniature. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's fine. I wasn't planning on going anyway. Besides, Ann's outfit was probably going to be too revealing for a family event.

jokes.text: Leslie shows her elaborate map of Greg Pikitis's routes to the statue. Dave: 'That looks like something you would find on the wall of a serial killer.'
jokes.setup: Leslie proudly presents her detailed surveillance map of possible routes from a teenager's house to a statue
jokes.punchline: Dave flatly observes it looks like a serial killer's obsession wall
jokes.explanation: The 'serial killer wall' comparison is a familiar comedic frame but it lands because of the setup — a government employee obsessing over a teenager's Halloween prank. Good economy. Leslie's response ('In a way, that's a compliment') is what elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: This is just like serial killer evidence boards.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Thank you!

jokes.text: Leslie's response to 'serial killer wall' comparison: 'In a way, that's a compliment. Shows dedication.'
jokes.setup: Dave has just compared Leslie's surveillance map to a serial killer's obsession wall
jokes.punchline: Leslie genuinely takes it as a compliment about her work ethic
jokes.explanation: This is excellent Leslie character comedy. Her genuine interpretation of 'serial killer' as a compliment to her dedication is perfectly in-character and reveals her entire worldview in five words. Strong character integration — only Leslie would process this comparison this way. Very economical.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. The practical reasons are... there are none. This is purely personal. Greg did me wrong, and I'm going to spend the next several years making sure he pays for it.

jokes.text: Leslie on why catching Pikitis matters: 'More importantly, Greg Pikitis sucks, and I wanna destroy him.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been framing her vendetta in professional terms (10 days to clean up, etc.)
jokes.punchline: She drops the professional framing entirely: 'Greg Pikitis sucks, and I wanna destroy him'
jokes.explanation: A great little admission that undercuts all her professional rationalization. The bluntness of 'sucks' from earnest Leslie is funny, and 'wanna destroy him' echoes her earlier dramatic threats. Strong economy — the brevity is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: He saved his grandmother's recipe during that deadly fire. That's the kind of leadership we need.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wasn't there like 30 people who died in that fire?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, but he wasn't Superman. You can't save everyone.

jokes.text: Leslie presents the statue of Mayor Percy — a description of heroism that gets undercut: 'During the Pawnee Bread Factory fire of 1922, he ran back into a burning building and saved the beloved secret recipe for Pawnee Pumpernickel.'
jokes.setup: Leslie introduces the statue as a monument to 'one of Pawnee's greatest mayors' and 'a true hero'
jokes.punchline: His heroic act was saving a bread recipe, not people
jokes.explanation: Strong Pawnee world-building joke — the absurdity that a mayor is celebrated for saving a pumpernickel recipe from a fire is rich with local-government satire. 'Beloved secret recipe for Pawnee Pumpernickel' is a funny phrase on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey, doesn't that statue kind of look like Ron?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, I literally just said that. Were you not listening to me at all?

jokes.text: Someone asks: 'Didn't, like, 30 people die in that fire?' Leslie: 'He wasn't Superman.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just praised Mayor Percy for running into a burning building to save a bread recipe
jokes.punchline: When challenged that 30 people died, Leslie's defense is 'He wasn't Superman' — fully accepting the deaths as acceptable while defending the recipe rescue
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Three words — 'He wasn't Superman' — do enormous comedic work. It's a completely reasonable-sounding non-defense that inadvertently accepts 30 deaths as fine while implying the bread recipe was the priority. Leslie delivers it earnestly, which makes it funnier. Perfect economy (10/10), strong character integration (Leslie's civic boosterism blinds her to the dark reality), highly quotable. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I just want to thank everyone for this amazing opportunity. I've been doing some calculations, and I figure with my new salary, I can finally afford the things I've always dreamed about.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: First, I'm gonna buy a new pair of shoes. That's gonna cost about $60. Then I'm gonna take a girl out to dinner at a real restaurant, not just Sweetums. That's gonna be another $40.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And then, I'm gonna have $3 left over, which means I can finally afford to buy that premium ice cream instead of the store brand. So in total, I'll have spent $103, which is way less than my $500 salary, so I'll still have $200 left to save.

jokes.text: Upon seeing the statue: 'He looks like Ron Swanson. Is that who this is based on?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is introducing Andy to the statue of Mayor Percy with great reverence
jokes.punchline: Andy notices the statue looks like Ron Swanson — a visual gag that also punctures Leslie's solemnity
jokes.explanation: A visual gag that works better on screen (seeing the statue actually resembles Nick Offerman). Functionally funny and in-character for Andy, but depends heavily on the visual payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're a doctor.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Harris
dialogue.line: I got it.

jokes.text: Leslie deputizes Andy with escalating contradictory instructions: 'Knock his head off if you have to.' / 'Don't do that.' / 'I give you permission to use excessive force.' / 'Don't use excessive force.' / 'By any means necessary.' / 'No. No.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving Andy official instructions for guarding the statue
jokes.punchline: Every violent/illegal instruction Leslie gives, Dave immediately contradicts — creating a rapid-fire contradiction loop that reveals Leslie's actual intentions
jokes.explanation: A well-structured escalation bit — the rhythm of Leslie's increasingly illegal instructions being immediately shot down by Dave builds nicely. The pattern itself becomes the joke, and Andy standing there absorbing all of it is great. Good character integration for all three.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm literally the only person in this office who has a normal relationship with someone outside of work. Everyone else is either dating their coworker or married to them or... I don't know, in some weird emotional entanglement I don't fully understand.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head: 'A week ago I had nothing. Now, I have a part-time job. I'm gonna make $32 tonight. I owe Leslie everything I have. Which, after tonight, will be $39.'
jokes.setup: Andy is reflecting on Leslie giving him a job guarding the statue
jokes.punchline: His total net worth will be $39 — the pathetically small sum makes the heartfelt sentiment both touching and tragic
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is perfect: a sincere, touching statement ('I owe Leslie everything I have') immediately undermined by the revelation that everything he has is $7, and after tonight it'll be $39. The math works out ($8/hr × 4 hours = $32, plus $7 existing = $39) which rewards attentive viewers. Deeply character-specific — only Andy's life situation makes this joke possible. Genuinely funny and a little heartbreaking simultaneously, which is Parks and Rec's sweet spot.

jokes.text: Ron meets Ann's date Dr. Harris in costume. Ann: 'This is Dr. Harris.' Ron: 'You're a doctor.' Dr. Harris: 'Yup.' Ron: 'I meant your costume.'
jokes.setup: Ron meets Ann's doctor friend at a Halloween party and states 'You're a doctor'
jokes.punchline: When Dr. Harris confirms it, Ron clarifies he meant the costume — implying the doctor came as a doctor for Halloween
jokes.explanation: A crisp, well-structured Halloween party joke. The misunderstanding beats perfectly — Ron's flat delivery of 'I meant your costume' lands hard because of the setup's ambiguity. Ron's deadpan makes it land exactly right. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: It's okay that you didn't wear a costume.

dialogue.speaker: Derek
dialogue.line: What do you mean? I am wearing a costume.

dialogue.speaker: Derek
dialogue.line: I'm being straight.

jokes.text: Ann's talking-head reaction after Ron's 'I meant your costume' exchange: 'Worlds colliding, always awkward.'
jokes.setup: The painfully awkward interaction between Ron and Ann's hospital friend at a Halloween party
jokes.punchline: Ann's resigned, understated assessment to the camera: 'Worlds colliding, always awkward'
jokes.explanation: A functional talking-head button that acknowledges the awkward moment. Not particularly original but serves its structural purpose. The delivery would carry this more than the writing.

jokes.text: Dave's talking head: 'Normally, I hate working on Halloween, but it's nice hanging out with Leslie. You know, she's focused, she's committed... And she made out with me in my cop car, which is pretty neat.'
jokes.setup: Dave gives what seems like a sincere, professional assessment of Leslie as a colleague
jokes.punchline: He casually drops that she made out with him in his cop car, then catches himself
jokes.explanation: Classic talking-head overshare structure done well. The pivot from professional praise to 'she made out with me in my cop car, which is pretty neat' is a funny tonal drop, and 'which is pretty neat' is a perfectly dorky Dave phrase. The self-aware 'I shouldn't have said that' button is solid.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Mark, you're an idiot. Andy is twice the man you'll ever be, and Ann deserves better than your incompetence. Stay away from her.

jokes.text: Dave's immediate follow-up: 'I shouldn't have said that. That's clear to me now.'
jokes.setup: Dave has just overshared that Leslie made out with him in his cop car
jokes.punchline: His delayed self-awareness — 'That's clear to me now' — implies it wasn't clear BEFORE he said it
jokes.explanation: The button on the previous joke — 'That's clear to me now' is a funny slight delay in self-awareness. Good character voice for Dave who is earnest but not entirely self-aware.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: Is 'turdish' even a real word?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes it is. Turdish is a word. It's a real word. Turdish.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: You're just saying it now.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not just saying it. Turdish. Turdish is real.

jokes.text: Derek and Ben arrive. Ben: 'It's totally okay that you didn't wear a costume.' / Derek: 'I did. I'm a straight person.'
jokes.setup: Ben tells a guest it's okay they didn't wear a costume
jokes.punchline: The guest clarifies they ARE in costume — as 'a straight person' — a gay man's costume is performing heterosexuality
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical joke. The setup ('it's okay you didn't wear a costume') feels like genuine consideration, and 'I'm a straight person' as the costume reveal is clever, character-specific, and lands with a great twist. One of the tightest joke constructions in the episode. Highly quotable and not hacky.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: JERRRRRRYYY!!!

jokes.text: Tom describing the gay Halloween party he passed up: 'Last year, I saw three Jonas Brothers make out with three Robert Pattinsons. It was amazing.'
jokes.setup: Tom is lamenting passing up a gay Halloween party to attend Ann's party
jokes.punchline: He describes a specific and glorious tableau from last year's gay party: 'three Jonas Brothers make out with three Robert Pattinsons'
jokes.explanation: Tom's specific, loving detail about the gay Halloween party is funny because of its specificity and his genuine wistfulness. The pairing of Jonas Brothers and Robert Pattinson (both 2009-era cultural touchstones) is period-specific charm. 'It was amazing' closes it perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This peach pit is evidence of a serial killer. See how it's been carefully removed? That's his signature. He's taunting us.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, it's a peach pit.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A peach pit left at the crime scene. Ben, serial killers always leave something behind. It's psychological.

jokes.text: Ann's friends immediately preferring Andy over Mark: 'So, you're the Mark that Ann is dating.' / 'We're very protective of Ann... So you kind of dropped the ball with Andy then, didn't you?'
jokes.setup: Ann's gay friends meet her new boyfriend Mark for the first time
jokes.punchline: They immediately confront him about Ann's ex Andy — implying he's a downgrade
jokes.explanation: A solid cringe moment — the social awkwardness of Ann's friends preferring her ex to her current boyfriend to his face. Functional but not particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: This party sucks. I'm leaving.

jokes.text: Leslie's official surveillance log: 'Suspect laughing with friends and playing with his stupid skateboard in a snide, turdish manner.' Dave: 'Turdish?' Leslie: 'Yes. Like a turd. Like a little turd.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is maintaining a formal surveillance log on a teenager
jokes.punchline: Her official description includes 'turdish' — a made-up word that she then seriously defines
jokes.explanation: An excellent Leslie Knope joke. 'Turdish' is a perfect made-up adjective that sounds plausible enough for an official document while being completely absurd. Her straight-faced definition ('Yes. Like a turd. Like a little turd.') and the escalation 'like a little turd' are both funny. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific — only Leslie's obsessive professionalism mixed with personal hatred produces 'turdish' in an official log.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm just going to take this book... and this pen... and this decorative item... and this coffee mug.

jokes.text: Leslie's final radio log before leaving surveillance: 'Leaving location. Look at stupid suspect. I hate suspect.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been maintaining official surveillance log language throughout the stakeout
jokes.punchline: Her final log entry breaks entirely into pure personal animosity: 'Look at stupid suspect. I hate suspect.'
jokes.explanation: The log-entry framing collapsing into 'I hate suspect' is genuinely funny. The third-person 'suspect' makes the petulance funnier. Strong Leslie character voice — even her hatred is bureaucratically logged.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You have a really scary face.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I mean... in a good way? Like, intimidating. That's useful.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: I don't think that's better.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, no. You could be a cop. Or a debt collector. People would take you very seriously.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: Okay, you can stop now.

jokes.text: Leslie and Dave arrive at the Parks Department to find it vandalized. Leslie shouts 'PIKITIS!' into the empty, defaced office.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Dave discover the Parks office has been vandalized while they were on surveillance
jokes.punchline: Leslie screams 'PIKITIS!' into the empty building — her theatrical nemesis-cry undercut by the fact that she was completely outsmarted
jokes.explanation: A great structural payoff — Leslie's confident opening 'it ends today' is immediately and thoroughly humiliated. The primal scream of 'PIKITIS!' into an empty vandalized office is excellent visual/character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to communicate without anyone seeing us.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: What do you suggest?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We could use that window over there.

dialogue.speaker: Greg
dialogue.line: That's a regular window. Everyone can see through it.

jokes.text: Leslie presents evidence: 'This is his ace of spades. This is his calling card. This is what he leaves all his victims. And it's still warm.' Dave: 'Okay, go and arrest him.' Leslie: 'And send this to the lab.' Dave: 'We don't have a lab.'
jokes.setup: Leslie dramatically presents a peach pit as criminal evidence, complete with theatrical 'calling card' framing
jokes.punchline: Dave's flat 'We don't have a lab' deflates her CSI fantasy entirely
jokes.explanation: The 'calling card... still warm' theatrical buildup punctured by 'We don't have a lab' is a clean structure. Leslie's TV-cop fantasy meeting small-town reality is a recurring comic engine that works here.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I mess with her because... [makes exaggerated impression of Leslie's angry face]

jokes.text: April arrives at Ann's party. Ann: 'Okay, you're underage.' April looks at Ann's date. Ann: 'You're not.' Mark awkwardly: 'Hey.'
jokes.setup: April shows up at a party where she's underage and there's alcohol
jokes.punchline: Ann makes the age distinction explicitly — April is underage, her adult date is not — creating an awkward beat as Ann essentially calls out April's inappropriateness while Mark says an ineffectual 'hey'
jokes.explanation: A mild cringe beat. April's transgression is barely registered before being moved past. The joke is more situational than written.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: What kind of candy do you like?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, I can't eat chocolate anymore. It goes right through me. And not in a good way.

jokes.text: April: 'This isn't that fun.' Ann: 'Didn't need to tell me that.' April takes a bottle and a book: 'I'm gonna take this home. Nobody was drinking it, so I'm gonna take it... Gonna take this, too. Been meaning to read it.'
jokes.setup: April has arrived at Ann's party and finds it boring
jokes.punchline: She casually begins taking Ann's things as she leaves — a bottle and a book — with matter-of-fact explanations that make the theft sound perfectly reasonable
jokes.explanation: Excellent April Ludgate character comedy. Her casual theft of Ann's belongings while explaining why each theft is justified ('nobody was drinking it,' 'been meaning to read it') is deeply specific to April's apathetic sociopathy. Ann's pained 'didn't need to tell me that' is the perfect straight-man response.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm Special Agent Bert Macklin, FBI. And you're under arrest for being a jerk.

jokes.text: Leslie tells Dave to question Pikitis: 'You have a scary face.' Dave: 'Hey. No, in a good way.' 'Scary cute.' Dave: 'Yeah?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving Dave a compliment to motivate him to interrogate a teenager
jokes.punchline: Her 'scary face' pivot to 'scary cute' as damage control, and Dave's earnest 'Yeah?' — a small relationship comedy beat
jokes.explanation: A small, warm relationship moment that's lightly funny. Dave's hopeful 'Yeah?' is sweet. Not a big laugh but a pleasant character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. I respect my wife's body and her right to dress however she wants. She's a strong, independent woman. But also, she's got great boobs and I'm very lucky.

jokes.text: In the interrogation room, Leslie holds up a sign from the other side of the glass: 'Ask him about the peach pit.' Greg: 'This isn't one-way glass, you know. I can see you.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to orchestrate the interrogation from behind what she believes is a one-way mirror
jokes.punchline: Greg casually informs her it's regular glass — she's been visible the whole time
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed visual gag. The setup of Leslie holding up a sign like a coaching session is funny on its own, but Greg's calm 'I can see you' — implying she's been doing this for a while — makes it funnier. Extends the running theme of Greg being smarter than Leslie at every turn.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy
dialogue.line: Well, I figured you'd want to be the only one dressed as a sexy professional.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm dressed as a character from a book.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy
dialogue.line: Yeah, a sexy character from a book.

jokes.text: Greg in interrogation: 'I screw with her 'cause she gets all riled up, and her face gets all scrunched up like this.' (Presumably makes a Leslie face)
jokes.setup: Greg explains his motivation for messing with Leslie
jokes.punchline: He demonstrates her 'scrunched up face' — a teenager doing an impression of a parks official while being interrogated
jokes.explanation: A character-driven moment where Greg's genuine affection for Leslie (despite the pranks) comes through. Mostly a visual gag — the physical impression is where the laugh lives. Also provides thematic warmth to Greg's character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to ask you some questions, and I need you to answer me honestly. This is serious.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A teenager's life could be at stake here.

jokes.text: Ann's party is failing. She's standing alone amid elaborate decorations while everyone clusters in the kitchen: 'I spent the whole day decorating this place, and everybody's in the kitchen. Why is everyone always in the kitchen?'
jokes.setup: Ann's Halloween party appears dead despite her effort
jokes.punchline: Her desperate 'Why is everyone always in the kitchen?' is an immediately relatable party-host grievance
jokes.explanation: A relatable observational joke about party dynamics. Not especially original but the character context (Ann's perfectionism vs. reality) gives it a bit more charge.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I have definitive proof right here. Fruit doesn't lie.

dialogue.speaker: Greg
dialogue.line: Actually, that's a kumquat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: What? No, this is clearly a—

dialogue.speaker: Greg
dialogue.line: You've been arguing about a kumquat this whole time.

jokes.text: Andy, guarding the statue, radios in: 'Hey, I'm here. Statue's fine. "Crappy Hallowieners." That's hilarious. Where's the kid?'
jokes.setup: Andy is supposedly on guard, surveilling the statue
jokes.punchline: He reads the vandalism on a nearby sign, laughs at it ('That's hilarious'), then asks where the kid is — completely missing that the vandalism IS the crime he's preventing, meaning he arrived after the fact
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly economical Andy joke. His oblivious appreciation of the vandalism he was supposed to prevent, delivered in an official radio tone, is perfect character comedy. 'That's hilarious' landing before 'Where's the kid?' makes the structural reveal land hard. Only Andy would laugh at the crime before noticing it IS the crime.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I followed you for three blocks!

dialogue.speaker: Greg
dialogue.line: Yeah, and you didn't see me commit any crimes. So technically, this proves I'm innocent.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not how this works!

jokes.text: Andy volunteers to interrogate Greg: 'Why don't you let me take a run at him, boss? In order to think like one of these guys, you have to think like them.'
jokes.setup: The adults have failed to break Greg in interrogation
jokes.punchline: Andy offers his 'profiling' wisdom: 'In order to think like one of these guys, you have to think like them' — a tautology delivered with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: Andy's tautological profiling advice ('to think like one of these guys, you have to think like them') delivered with total confidence is an excellent absurdist character joke. It sounds like something Andy genuinely believes is profound. The perfect non-insight delivered as deep wisdom — highly characteristic of Andy and very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to torture you.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: I'm concerned that's a serious threat.

jokes.text: Leslie gestures toward pliers on the table during the interrogation. Dave: 'Look, I'm not gonna torture this kid.' Leslie: 'Nobody said torture.'
jokes.setup: Leslie wants a confession from Greg and has gestured meaningfully at pliers
jokes.punchline: The immediate denial of torture ('nobody said torture') implicitly confirms torture was exactly what was implied
jokes.explanation: Classic comedic denial. 'Nobody said torture' is funnier because someone clearly implied it. The pliers as prop (visual) combined with Leslie's reasonable-sounding denial makes this darkly funny. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ladies and gentlemen, please welcome to the stage... ROOOOOOOON SWANSON!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Introducing you like the legend you are, baby!

jokes.text: Andy enters the interrogation room as 'Bert Macklin, FBI,' opens with: 'Would you like some boiling hot coffee in your face?'
jokes.setup: Andy is supposed to imply he's someone important who can make Greg's life hell
jokes.punchline: His opening gambit as 'Bert Macklin, FBI' is offering Greg boiling hot coffee in his face — the most bizarre possible interrogation opener
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top moments. 'Bert Macklin, FBI' is an instantly iconic Andy character bit, and 'Would you like some boiling hot coffee in your face?' as his opening interrogation line is perfectly deranged. It's both threatening-sounding and completely absurd — Andy apparently thinks this is how FBI agents work. The character integration is as high as it gets: only Andy Dwyer/Bert Macklin would open with this. Extremely quotable and a clear rewatch highlight.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We're with the FBI.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Federal Bureau of Investigation.

jokes.text: Andy: 'My name is Bert Macklin. I'm with the FBI.' Greg immediately ignores him and asks: 'Ooh. Are these the same kind of chips?'
jokes.setup: Andy has just delivered his dramatic FBI introduction
jokes.punchline: Greg completely ignores the intimidation attempt to ask about snacks — demonstrating both Greg's total unflappability and Andy's failure as an interrogator
jokes.explanation: Greg's instant pivot to snacks after Andy's dramatic FBI declaration is a great reaction beat. The best possible response to Andy's intimidation is indifference, and the specificity of 'are these the same kind of chips?' makes it funnier than a generic dismissal.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Pikitis
dialogue.line: Who should I call about Leslie?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The President.

jokes.text: Tom arrives at Ann's party as T-Pain: 'Ann! What's up, gorgeous! Get your Raggedy ass over here, girl.' Then singing: 'She poppin', she rollin', she rollin', she climbin' that pole and I'm in love with a stripper.'
jokes.setup: Ann's party is dying and she needs help
jokes.punchline: Tom arrives fully committed to T-Pain, including Autotune delivery and strip club lyrics, instantly changing the energy — in front of Tom's surgeon wife
jokes.explanation: Tom's full T-Pain commitment is fun character comedy — he's exactly the kind of person who would go all-in on this costume and this entrance. The context of him singing about strippers before introducing his wife makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Dave
dialogue.line: I'm sorry for the bad police work.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, that's okay. I'm sorry for the equally fake FBI work.

jokes.text: Tom: 'This is not a stripper. It's my wife, Wendy. You remember her? She's a surgeon at County General, and she's super hot.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just sung 'I'm in love with a stripper' and is now introducing his wife
jokes.punchline: His clarification ('not a stripper, it's my wife') followed immediately by 'she's super hot' suggests he's more impressed by her hotness than her surgical career
jokes.explanation: Tom's ordering of 'surgeon at County General... and she's super hot' with emphasis clearly on the latter is good character comedy. His shallow priorities are consistently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Alright, next up, we got a real treat. This is from the rap legend himself, Notorious B.I.G. — or as I like to call him, Notorious M.O.D., which stands for 'Man Of Distinction.'

jokes.text: Dr. Harris (in a doctor costume at a party with a surgeon): 'Well, thank you for being a doctor and not coming dressed as a doctor.' Wendy: 'Oh, my God. Who'd be boring enough to do that?' — Then realizes.
jokes.setup: At Ann's Halloween party, the callback to 'I meant your costume' — Dr. Harris compliments Wendy for not coming as a doctor
jokes.punchline: Wendy, who IS a doctor and presumably IS wearing a doctor costume, responds with 'Who'd be boring enough to do that?' before presumably realizing
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback to the earlier doctor-costume joke. Wendy's oblivious 'who'd be boring enough' before presumably realizing she IS dressed as a doctor is a good cringe beat. The callback structure rewards attentive viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You didn't do stupid stuff in high school. You were a nerd.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I mean, not a nerd nerd. Like a cool nerd. A nerd-cool.

jokes.text: Ann's party continues to fail. Tom: 'Ann, what happened here? Did you tell everyone they're gonna have to get a bone marrow transplant tomorrow? They look miserable.'
jokes.setup: Tom surveys Ann's dead party
jokes.punchline: His specific medical metaphor — 'did you tell everyone they're gonna get a bone marrow transplant tomorrow?' — for why everyone looks miserable is a Tom-specific absurd observation
jokes.explanation: Tom's bone marrow transplant comparison is specific enough to be funny. The medical specificity (not just 'bad news' but a particularly grueling procedure) shows good comedy writing instincts.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy
dialogue.line: I want you to come back to my place.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: What? No, I can't do that.

dialogue.speaker: Wendy
dialogue.line: It was a test. I was testing you.

jokes.text: Andy's interrogation falls apart. Greg: 'That is the dumbest thing I've ever heard.' Andy screams: 'WHY DON'T YOU JUST SHUT UP FOR A SECOND?' Greg: 'He's being such a jerk!' Andy: 'That's an awful thing to say to a human being!' / 'Are you crying?' Andy: 'I am NOT crying, okay? I'm ALLERGIC TO JERKS!'
jokes.setup: Andy's FBI interrogation has devolved; the interrogatee and interrogator are now fighting like children
jokes.punchline: Andy's defense: 'I'm allergic to jerks!' — a ludicrous physical alibi for crying that also reveals he's been completely destabilized by a teenager
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke. The escalation from Andy's confident FBI opener to him crying and screaming 'I'M ALLERGIC TO JERKS' at a teenager is a perfect comedic arc. 'I'm allergic to jerks' is an inspired line — it's simultaneously a weak denial of crying, a childlike physical claim, and a perfect encapsulation of Andy's emotional immaturity. The sequence earns the escalation completely. Extremely quotable, deeply character-specific, and one of the most memorable moments in the episode. Comparable to the high anchor examples.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm sorry to hear that, Wendy. That sounds terrible. But you know what? That's what happens when you have socialized medicine.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head after Andy's interrogation: 'Okay. The gloves are coming off.'
jokes.setup: Andy has completely failed at interrogation and had a breakdown
jokes.punchline: Leslie, undeterred, announces 'The gloves are coming off' — as if Andy's performance was just a warm-up
jokes.explanation: A functional button on the Andy interrogation sequence. The pomposity of 'gloves are coming off' after that disaster is mildly funny. Workmanlike.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so Greg's committed identity theft, wire fraud, and he TP'd the Sweetums building.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: He also TP'd the library. Twice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: He TP'd my house while I was home.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And he TP'd the Nuttercutters factory during business hours.

jokes.text: Leslie tries her peach pit evidence on Greg. Greg: 'Wow, you nailed me. I mean, there's no way that two different people could have eaten the same fruit in the same day, in the same area of Indiana. Never mind that I was actually eating a plum when you saw me earlier.'
jokes.setup: Leslie triumphantly presents the peach pit as damning evidence
jokes.punchline: Greg methodically dismantles the 'evidence' with devastating teenage sarcasm, then drops that it wasn't even a peach — it was a plum
jokes.explanation: An excellent structural callback payoff. The 'two different people could eat the same fruit... in Indiana' logic is sharp teenage sarcasm, and the final reveal — it wasn't even a peach, it was a plum — is a perfect twist that retroactively makes Leslie's entire evidence theory even more embarrassing. Strong structure with a satisfying escalating punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is the most fun I've had since... well, since the last time I did this. Which was last week.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But I want to be clear: toilet papering someone's house is wrong. It's destructive, it's wasteful, and it's disrespectful to private property.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That said, look at how perfectly this tree is draped. *chef's kiss*

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I don't care that you were in the parking lot all night.' Greg: 'Wait — how did you know I was in the parking lot all night?' Leslie: 'Because I followed you, genius!' Greg: 'If you followed me all night, then you know it wasn't me.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is aggressively asserting Greg's guilt
jokes.punchline: In her passion, she accidentally proves his alibi — she followed him all night and therefore can confirm he wasn't at the Parks office
jokes.explanation: Structurally, this might be the tightest joke in the episode. Leslie's passion causes her to accidentally establish Greg's alibi — the very thing she was doing to CATCH him is what CLEARS him. The irony is perfectly constructed, and Greg's calm 'if you followed me all night then you know it wasn't me' lands like a hammer. This is professional comedy writing: the setup is earned over the whole episode, and the payoff reveals character (Leslie's blind obsession defeats her). Approaches the very top of the craft scale.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm thinking about opening a new restaurant concept. High-end, but approachable. I'm calling it 'Rent's Too Damn High: A Gastropub.' We'll serve artisanal small plates and craft cocktails at prices that reflect the current real estate market.

jokes.text: Leslie, losing the argument: 'I have been very civil. But I will waterboard you.' Dave: 'No, no.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just been logically defeated by a teenager and is escalating
jokes.punchline: Her ultimate threat is waterboarding, delivered in the same tone as a normal negotiation position
jokes.explanation: Leslie threatening waterboarding in the same breath as 'I've been very civil' is a great incongruity joke — her cheerful earnestness applied to an illegal interrogation technique. Dave's weary 'no, no' is the perfect response.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, who is this?

dialogue.speaker: Greg
dialogue.line: This is my mom.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But I thought your mom was... I met your mom last month at the thing.

dialogue.speaker: Greg
dialogue.line: Yeah, that was my fake mom. This is my real mom. I have seven fake parents I rotate through for different situations.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Greg
dialogue.line: Sympathy. People give you things if your parents are weird.

jokes.text: Dave's talking head about Leslie's interrogation: 'I don't think she would make a good cop. I would be frightened to live in a town that she's the cop of, frankly.'
jokes.setup: We've just watched Leslie threaten to waterboard a teenager
jokes.punchline: Dave's understated assessment: he would be 'frightened to live in a town that she's the cop of'
jokes.explanation: A functional talking-head button. Dave's police perspective on Leslie's 'interrogation' is a good straight-man observation. The construction 'town that she's the cop of' is slightly clunky but the sentiment lands.

dialogue.speaker: Greg Pikitis's Mother
dialogue.line: You told them I was dead?!

dialogue.speaker: Greg Pikitis
dialogue.line: Mom, let me explain—

dialogue.speaker: Greg Pikitis's Mother
dialogue.line: You had someone PRETEND to be me?! Who does that?!

jokes.text: Tom takes over Ann's party: 'All right, y'all! Take the pigs in the blanket and put them to sleep! It's time to get wild! Get this furniture out of here, y'all, we're making a dance floor. Come on, y'all. Put the turkey wraps down. We're about to get wild.'
jokes.setup: Ann's party is dead; Tom and Ron are given carte blanche to fix it
jokes.punchline: Tom's DJ/hype-man persona — commanding people to 'put the turkey wraps down' and 'put the pigs in blankets to sleep' — treating party food like obstacles to wildness
jokes.explanation: 'Put the turkey wraps down' as a party command is a funny specific detail. Tom's hype-man energy is solid character comedy, though it's more effective on screen than on the page.

dialogue.speaker: Greg
dialogue.line: That was some impressive detective work, Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Thanks, Greg. I've been working on my investigative skills.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Unlike you, who couldn't investigate your way out of a paper bag if it had instructions written on it.

jokes.text: Tom at the revived party: 'Ron Swanson's in the building, y'all!'
jokes.setup: Tom is hyping up the party; Ron Swanson has presumably started dancing or done something unexpected
jokes.punchline: The announcement of Ron Swanson as a party highlight — the least likely man to be a dance-floor presence — is itself the joke
jokes.explanation: Five words that do enormous work. 'Ron Swanson's in the building, y'all!' as a party announcement is funny on its own because Ron is the last person anyone would expect to be announced at a party. The visual of Ron presumably doing something absurdly Ron-like on a dance floor elevates it further.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're telling me that's actually how you organize your files?

dialogue.speaker: Greg
dialogue.line: Works for me.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: By just... naming everything after a turd?

dialogue.speaker: Greg
dialogue.line: I don't know what to tell you, Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's the worst filing system I've ever heard in my entire life.

jokes.text: Andy, still in character as Bert Macklin FBI, introduces himself to Greg's mom: 'Bert Macklin, FBI.'
jokes.setup: Greg's mom has arrived to rescue her son from illegal detention; Andy is present
jokes.punchline: Andy maintains the Bert Macklin bit even in this escalating serious situation
jokes.explanation: The callback to Bert Macklin is quick and effective. Andy's commitment to the bit in an increasingly serious situation is funny because he has no read on the room. Three words does it.

jokes.text: After the debacle, Leslie: 'Let them think they've lost us. Then we're...' Dave walks away: 'Where are you going?' / Dave: 'I gotta go tell my boss why I illegally detained a teenager.'
jokes.setup: The Pikitis situation has collapsed; Leslie is still in tactical mode
jokes.punchline: Dave calmly states he must now go face real consequences for their actions — completely breaking from Leslie's fantasy of continued pursuit
jokes.explanation: Good reality-check beat. Dave's exit is a nice contrast to Leslie's continuing tactical thinking. 'I illegally detained a teenager' is the right level of blunt.

jokes.text: Andy, still in character: 'Yeah, it was bad FBI work, too. My bad.'
jokes.setup: Dave has just said it was 'bad police work'
jokes.punchline: Andy accepts co-responsibility as a fake FBI agent, completely seriously
jokes.explanation: A perfect two-line joke. Andy's 'My bad' as a fake FBI agent — accepting genuine professional responsibility for made-up professional conduct — is precisely the right level of Andy Dwyer absurdism. The economy is exceptional: three words do everything.

jokes.text: After the party has been saved, Dave to Ron: 'Son. That is one hell of a costume.' Ron: 'Thanks.'
jokes.setup: Dave encounters Ron at the party after Ron has apparently been dancing/performing
jokes.punchline: Dave's genuine compliment of Ron's 'costume' — presumably Ron is just being himself and/or it's unclear what his costume is — and Ron's flat 'Thanks'
jokes.explanation: A small but pleasant Ron joke — the ambiguity about whether he's in costume or just being Ron is a good visual gag. Ron's monosyllabic 'Thanks' is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: Dave to Ron about the party: 'Why would anyone do this?' Ron: 'Kids are kids. Everybody does stupid stuff like this in high school.' Leslie: 'I didn't.' Dave: 'Yeah, but you were probably a nerd, though, huh?'
jokes.setup: Dave observes the chaos of a party and wonders why anyone would do this
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'I didn't' confirming she was a complete non-participant in normal teenage fun; Dave's 'you were probably a nerd' is the expected response, but his quick recovery ('I mean that in a good way') is the real beat
jokes.explanation: Leslie's instant 'I didn't' is a good character beat — she was exactly the kind of kid who didn't do stupid stuff and is proud of it. Dave's 'nerd' observation and fumbling recovery ('in a good way') is a sweet relationship moment with a mild laugh.

jokes.text: Dave's save attempt: 'Leslie, I mean that in a good way. Look at you now. You're the coolest person I've ever met. I even met John Cougar Mellencamp once.'
jokes.setup: Dave is trying to compliment Leslie after calling her a nerd
jokes.punchline: His highest compliment is comparing her favorably to John Cougar Mellencamp — establishing his cultural reference point as very Indiana and circa-1985
jokes.explanation: The John Cougar Mellencamp reference as the pinnacle of celebrity encounters is a perfect Indiana joke — he's the most culturally specific celebrity possible for this show's setting. Dave using him as the benchmark for 'cool' is a funny character detail.

jokes.text: Mark hits on Leslie while they're both at the party. Leslie realizes: 'What? No. I'm dating Ann.' Mark: 'Good. That was a test. You passed.' Leslie: 'Let's celebrate you passing the test, over a drink, at my place.' Mark: 'No. Still no.'
jokes.setup: Mark flirts with Leslie
jokes.punchline: His 'that was a test' recovery, then immediately repeating the line verbatim ('let's celebrate, at my place'), then Leslie's 'still no' and 'we're still watching you'
jokes.explanation: A good running-gag structure — Mark repeating the exact same line after 'that was a test' makes him look worse, and Leslie's 'still no' and 'we're watching you' (echoing the Greg Pikitis plot) is a nice cross-plot rhyme. The immediate double repeat is the comedic engine here.

jokes.text: Mark, completely undeterred, tries on a third woman: 'So, you wanna get out of here, go back to my place?' — directed at someone new at the party.
jokes.setup: Mark has just been rejected twice using the exact same line
jokes.punchline: He immediately tries again on a new person with the identical line — establishing it as a persistent character flaw/habit
jokes.explanation: The third use of the same line makes the running gag land — the repetition is the joke. By now we expect Mark to be shameless and the confirmation is satisfying.

jokes.text: Dr. Harris spots someone else at the party: 'So, you wanna get out of here, go back to my place?' — immediately trying the same line on a new person
jokes.setup: Dr. Harris has struck out twice using this exact line
jokes.punchline: He deploys the identical line on a third person immediately — showing the 'test' framing was just persistence under a new brand
jokes.explanation: The triple callback — same exact line, third person — is satisfying running gag structure. His persistence is the joke. Works well as a runner within the episode.

jokes.text: Wendy tells Ron she wants to thank him for not revealing their green card marriage. Ron: 'I'd hate for you to have to go back to Canada.' Beat. 'All that socialized medicine up there.'
jokes.setup: Wendy thanks Ron for keeping her secret green card marriage to Tom quiet
jokes.punchline: Ron says he'd hate for her to go back to Canada, then adds 'all that socialized medicine up there' — revealing his motivation isn't sympathy but libertarian horror at Canadian healthcare
jokes.explanation: A superb Ron Swanson joke. The setup suggests Ron's benevolence; the punchline reveals his true motivation is dread of socialized medicine — he's not protecting Wendy, he's protecting America from Canadian healthcare influence. The character integration is near-perfect: this joke could ONLY be Ron Swanson. The pause before 'all that socialized medicine up there' is where the laugh lives. Economy is excellent — the joke is complete in under 15 words.

jokes.text: Tom explains that he and Wendy plan to divorce soon: 'We'll invite you to the divorce party.'
jokes.setup: Tom explains their green card marriage will end soon
jokes.punchline: He announces there will be a divorce party — treating a legal dissolution like a social event worth celebrating with invitations
jokes.explanation: Only Tom Haverford would throw — and enthusiastically invite people to — a divorce party. Good character integration. The casualness of the invitation is the joke.

jokes.text: Dave's talking head: 'Huh, maybe Greg is innocent... On the other hand, Greg Pikitis is a little punk. And I kind of wanna TP his house.' Leslie: 'Let's do it.'
jokes.setup: Dave is reconsidering Greg's guilt after Leslie accidentally established his alibi
jokes.punchline: He acknowledges possible innocence, then immediately pivots to 'I kind of wanna TP his house' anyway
jokes.explanation: The police officer who just told Leslie she was doing bad police work immediately suggests doing the exact same thing they were trying to stop Greg from doing. The hypocrisy is the joke, and 'I kind of wanna TP his house' from a cop is inherently funny.

jokes.text: Leslie and Dave TPing Pikitis's house. Leslie: 'Wait, wait! Wait, wait! This is fun! This is fun! What do I do?' Dave walks her through it, then Leslie: 'This is for Mayor Percy! This is for the Parks Department office! This is for pooping on the handball court!'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Dave are toilet-papering a teenager's house for revenge
jokes.punchline: Leslie's dedication to naming each roll's purpose, culminating in 'This is for pooping on the handball court!' — an escalating list of grievances against Greg that gets increasingly petty
jokes.explanation: A wonderful Leslie escalation. The list structure works perfectly: 'Mayor Percy' (official, professional), 'Parks Department office' (still professional), 'POOPING ON THE HANDBALL COURT' (personal, disgusting, hilarious). The specificity of the handball court grievance and its casual placement as the climactic reason is great comedy writing. Leslie's 'this is fun! This is fun! What do I do?' before diving in with such commitment is perfect character work.

jokes.text: Leslie, mid-TP rampage: 'Yeah! This is really fun! But I don't condone it!'
jokes.setup: Leslie is joyfully TPing a house while providing a legal/ethical disclaimer
jokes.punchline: 'But I don't condone it!' — the civic employee in her cannot fully commit to lawbreaking without a caveat
jokes.explanation: One of the best Leslie jokes in the episode. 'This is really fun! But I don't condone it!' perfectly captures her entire character — her genuine joy in rebellion constrained by her civic duty instincts. She's having the time of her life while simultaneously issuing a public service disclaimer. The contrast is perfect, the economy is excellent, and it's extremely quotable. Could only be Leslie Knope.

jokes.text: Tom complimenting Mark about Wendy: 'I don't know how you landed that chick, but she's awesome.' Then catching himself: 'Nice work. You're lucky.'
jokes.setup: Tom is chatting with Mark about his wife Wendy
jokes.punchline: Tom accidentally implies he doesn't understand his own romantic success — then stiffly corrects to the more appropriate 'you're lucky' without fully walking back the original implication
jokes.explanation: A mild joke about Tom's green card marriage subtext — he can't quite bring himself to be humble about landing Wendy. Functional but not particularly sharp.

jokes.text: Mark says goodbye and announces: 'About to head home and have crazy sex.' Awkward beat. 'That's cool. I don't... Yeah!'
jokes.setup: Mark is saying goodnight to Ann's party guests
jokes.punchline: He overshares 'about to head home and have crazy sex,' then experiences an awkward beat as people react, then doubles down with a weird 'Yeah!'
jokes.explanation: A decent overshare cringe moment. The unnecessary announcement of 'crazy sex' to a group is mildly funny. The awkward 'Yeah!' recovery makes it slightly funnier.

jokes.text: Leslie and Dave are caught TPing the house. Someone shouts 'FIVE-O! FIVE-O!' from inside.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Dave are in the act of vandalizing Pikitis's house
jokes.punchline: 'Five-O!' — the classic warning that police are coming — shouted about the police officer who IS committing the vandalism
jokes.explanation: A clean irony joke — 'Five-O' is being shouted about the cop who is himself committing the crime. The inversion is funny and economical.

jokes.text: Andy is inside the Pikitis house watching through the window. Andy and Leslie make eye contact through the window. 'I see you in there, Andy.' 'Leslie? What are you doing?'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Dave are caught TPing a house
jokes.punchline: Andy is inexplicably inside the house, watching through the window — his presence there raises as many questions as it answers
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Andy is inside the Pikitis house — with no explanation of how or why — is a great visual gag. His 'Leslie? What are you doing?' as if she's the one in the wrong position is perfect. The mystery of Andy's presence makes this moment funnier than it should be.

jokes.text: Leslie explains to the actual Mrs. Pikitis that she has the wrong house: '...we were trying to get revenge on this kid, Greg Pikitis, and we thought this was his house, but I guess we got the address wrong.' Mrs. Pikitis: 'I'm Greg's mom.' Leslie: 'You are? ... Did he hire a fake mom again, to get him out of trouble?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is mortified to have TPed the wrong house; the homeowner reveals she's Greg's actual mother
jokes.punchline: Leslie's first instinct is not shame but suspicion — 'Did he hire a fake mom AGAIN?' — implying this is a known Greg Pikitis tactic she's aware of
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: mortifying reveal (wrong house, real mom) → Leslie's refusal to accept reality → 'did he hire a fake mom AGAIN?' The word 'again' does extraordinary work — it establishes that Greg's Craigslist-fake-mom gambit is a known repeat strategy, which retroactively makes him even more of a criminal genius than Leslie thought. Perfectly earned (the earlier interrogation scene planted the 'fake mom' concept) and hugely payoff-satisfying. Strong callback structure, excellent character integration.

jokes.text: The real Mrs. Pikitis: 'Whenever he gets in trouble, he goes on Craigslist and hires a woman to play his mother and bail him out.' Leslie: 'Oh, that little SOB!'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Pikitis explains that the 'fake mom' is a real Greg Pikitis strategy
jokes.punchline: Confirmation that Greg really does hire fake moms from Craigslist — a gloriously specific and absurd criminal scheme for a teenager
jokes.explanation: The confirmation that Craigslist fake moms is a real Greg Pikitis strategy is wonderfully specific and absurd. The specificity of 'goes on Craigslist' grounds the absurdity in contemporary reality in a way that makes it funnier. Leslie's 'Oh, that little SOB!' is the perfect reaction — half outrage, half impressed.

jokes.text: Greg is not in his room. Dave: 'He's not in his room. I don't know where he is.' Leslie: 'I do.'
jokes.setup: They've confirmed the Craigslist fake mom scheme — Greg has outsmarted them again
jokes.punchline: Leslie's knowing 'I do' — implying she finally has him figured out — sets up the final confrontation
jokes.explanation: A structural beat more than a joke — it sets up the chase sequence. Mildly satisfying as a reversal ('now I've got you') but not especially funny on its own.

jokes.text: After catching Greg: 'How did you get into the Parks Department? I have to know.' Greg: 'Maybe the FBI can figure it out.' Andy: 'I'm not even in the FBI, stupid.'
jokes.setup: Greg is caught; Leslie wants to understand how he pulled off the heist
jokes.punchline: Greg's sarcastic FBI reference prompts Andy to break the Bert Macklin fiction entirely: 'I'm not even in the FBI, stupid'
jokes.explanation: A satisfying Bert Macklin callback. Andy breaking the FBI character to call Greg 'stupid' — after having completely failed as an interrogator — is funny because it's the most Andy thing possible. He's breaking his cover to be petty. Greg's provocation is well-constructed to produce this exact response.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'You're going to jail for a very long time.' Dave: 'He's not gonna go to jail, you know. He's a minor.' Leslie: 'Well, we'll let the jury decide.' Dave: 'There's not gonna be a jury...' Leslie: 'Then the judge will decide where he goes.'
jokes.setup: Greg has been caught; Dave and Leslie discuss consequences
jokes.punchline: Leslie's legal understanding is entirely wrong, and she simply sidesteps each correction by moving the goalposts ('well, we'll let the jury decide' → 'then the JUDGE will decide')
jokes.explanation: A solid Leslie escalation bit — her willingness to accept each correction while immediately finding a new legal avenue (jury → judge) shows her refusal to accept reality while technically acknowledging it. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Dave: 'He's going to do probation, he's a minor.' Leslie: 'Dave, just let me have this.'
jokes.setup: Dave is explaining the actual legal consequences for a juvenile vandal
jokes.punchline: 'Dave, just let me have this' — Leslie abandoning all legal pretense and openly asking for an emotional victory
jokes.explanation: A beautiful Leslie line. After all the threats of juries, judges, and waterboarding, her final ask is simply 'just let me have this' — openly admitting she wants the emotional satisfaction more than any actual justice. The economy is excellent (six words that reveal her entire motivation), and it's deeply character-specific. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Dave's talking head: 'Wow. Nice work, Knope.' Leslie: 'Yeah. That is amazing.' Then immediately: 'Thanks. But the thing that's driving me nuts is, how did he do it?'
jokes.setup: They've caught Greg Pikitis; Dave and Leslie are reflecting on the victory
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately pivots from victory to obsessing over how Greg pulled it off — she can't enjoy the win without solving the puzzle
jokes.explanation: A good character coda — Leslie cannot just enjoy the win, she immediately needs to understand Greg's method. This reveals her obsessive mind and also sets up the final mysterious tag. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Leslie, at the end: 'The thing that's driving me nuts is, how did he do it? If you destroy him early, please come by.' Then the episode cuts to replaying Leslie's own flashback clue: 'How is someone gonna be able to get through that door?'
jokes.setup: Greg has been caught but the method of the original office break-in remains unexplained
jokes.punchline: The episode replays the moment where Leslie herself left the door open ('Oh!' / 'What the...') — suggesting Leslie accidentally let Greg in earlier
jokes.explanation: The episode's structural comedy payoff. The callback to 'How is someone gonna get through that door?' — with the implication that the answer is 'because you left it open, Leslie' — is a perfectly constructed mystery punchline. It rewards attentive viewers and recontextualizes the entire episode. Gets a high structure score because this requires planting the clue and paying it off, which is proper comedy architecture. Earns 8+ because it's a rare example of sitcom plot-level joke construction.

jokes.text: The final tag: Leslie, Dave, Andy puzzling over how Greg got in. A replay of earlier office footage: 'First of all, we always lock the doors when we leave.' 'And Dave and I tailed Pikitis from the moment he left his house at 7:00 p.m.' 'Does he have a lookalike?' 'Did he have an accomplice?' / 'How did that little turd do it?'
jokes.setup: Greg has been caught for the crime, but no one can figure out HOW he did it
jokes.punchline: The episode ends without an answer — Greg Pikitis remains a criminal mastermind even in defeat. The mystery is never solved. Leslie's final 'how did that little turd do it?' is the last line.
jokes.explanation: A strong episode-closing joke that pays off the central premise — even caught, Greg Pikitis remains a mystery. The decision to NOT explain how he did it is a bold comedic choice that validates Leslie's 'James Bond super villain' description from the opening. 'How did that little turd do it?' is a callback to 'turdish' and closes the episode on exactly the right note. The unresolved mystery is itself the joke: Leslie wins the battle but Greg wins the war of mystique.

tmdb_overview: Leslie enlists the help of Dave and Andy in order to catch a local teen vandal. Meanwhile, Ann struggles to make her Halloween party fun, and ends up getting help from an unlikely source.
insight: Halloween prank obsession escalates absurdly; 49 jokes in 24 minutes fuels Season 2's momentum shift.
